title: Undefined behaviour
objectives: Spot undefined behaviour in short snippets and say what the compiler may do with it.

screens.title: The check that vanished
screens.prose: This app never runs undefined behaviour: whatever happens is allowed, so the answer could differ by build. These screens show code and compiler output, and you judge.
screens.question: Why is there no null test in the output?

options.text: It had already read `*p`, so it assumed `p` is not null
The optimiser removes every `if` it can
options.why: It dropped one comparison it could prove, not every `if`.
A program that breaks the rules has no wrong answer, so this is not a compiler bug.
`nullptr` is a real value. The compiler assumed it away only after the read.

hints.text: Look at the order of lines 2 and 3.
The read comes before the test.
Reading through a null pointer is undefined, so the compiler may assume it never happens.

feedback.correct: The read came first, so the test after it could never be needed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the order of the read and the test.

byKey.drops: You thought it removes every `if`. It dropped one comparison it could prove.
byKey.bug: A program that breaks the rules has no wrong answer, so this is not a compiler bug.
byKey.never: `nullptr` is a real value. The compiler assumed it away only after the read.

explain.text: Reading `*p` is undefined for null, so the compiler may assume `p` is not null from line 2 on. The later test is then always false, and it is deleted.

screens.title: Which lines are undefined?
screens.prose: Eight lines, one function. Unsigned arithmetic and signed arithmetic differ. In the standard this app uses, reading a variable before it is set is undefined.
screens.question: Tap every line with undefined behaviour.

hints.text: Ask of each line: does the standard define the result?
Line 3 wraps by definition.
Lines 4, 6 and 8: one past the end, an unset variable, a signed overflow.

feedback.correct: Lines 4, 6 and 8: an index past the end, an unset read and a signed overflow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only some arithmetic is left undefined by the standard.

byKey.with-unsigned: You tapped line 3. Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition: `u - 1` is 4,294,967,295. Only signed overflow is undefined.
byKey.no-uninit: You left out line 6. Reading `x` before it is set is undefined, not just a garbage value.
byKey.no-index: You left out line 4. `a[3]` is one past the end of a 3-element array.

explain.text: Line 3 wraps to 4,294,967,295, which is defined. Lines 4, 6 and 8 have no defined result, so the compiler may assume they never run.

screens.title: Three kinds of unclear
screens.prose: Defined means one answer. Implementation-defined means the compiler documents its choice, and unspecified means it may pick either. Undefined means no promise at all.
screens.question: Drag each snippet to its kind.

hints.text: Start with the ones that wrap or round by a fixed rule.
Sizes and the sign of a plain `char` depend on the platform.
Anything that overflows a signed type, indexes past the end, or reads an unset variable is undefined.

feedback.correct: Two defined, three left to the compiler, four undefined.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort by who decides the result: the standard, the compiler or nobody.

byKey.t1: `UINT_MAX + 1u` is 0: unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition.
byKey.t2: `-7 / 2` is -3: division rounds towards zero since C++11.
byKey.t3: `sizeof(long)` is 4 here and 8 on a desktop: the compiler documents it.
byKey.t4: Whether plain `char` is signed depends on the platform, so the compiler documents it.
byKey.t5: The standard leaves the order of evaluation of arguments unspecified: either may run first.
byKey.t6: Signed overflow is undefined: the standard puts no limit on what follows.
byKey.t7: An index past the end is undefined, even if the memory happens to exist.
byKey.t8: Reading an unset `int` is undefined, not just a garbage value.
byKey.t9: Shifting by the width of the type or more is undefined.

explain.text: Defined: one answer. Implementation-defined or unspecified: a choice that does not break the program. Undefined: the whole run loses its guarantees.

screens.title: Making it report
screens.prose: These lines come from a desk machine running g++, not from this app. This app compiles with libc++ hardening on, which stops an out-of-range vector index, but it cannot see an overflow or a null read.

lines: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'
runtime error: index 3 out of bounds for type 'int [3]'
runtime error: load of null pointer of type 'volatile int'
params.title: desk machine, g++, not this app

screens.question: Which flag turns these reports on?

options.why: `-Wall` warns at compile time. It cannot see values that only exist at run time.
A lower optimisation level changes what happens. It does not report anything.
`-g` adds line numbers to reports but turns none on.

hints.text: The reports appear while the program runs.
One flag instruments the code to check each operation.
It is spelt `-fsanitize=` followed by the checker.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which flag adds checks that run with the program?

byKey.wall: You chose `-Wall`. It warns at compile time and cannot see run-time values.
byKey.o0: You chose `-O0`. A lower level changes what happens but reports nothing.
byKey.g: You chose `-g`. It adds line numbers to reports but turns none on.

explain.text: The sanitiser instruments each risky operation and prints the line when one is undefined. Add `-fsanitize=address` for memory errors such as a read past a heap block.

screens.title: A check that is defined
screens.prose: Return `true` when `a + b` does not fit in an `int`. The starter looks at the sum after it has overflowed. Your check must never overflow itself.
screens.question: Rewrite `add_overflows` so the addition never happens.

widget.how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer is `true` when `a + b` does not fit in an `int`, and every test uses values the correct check handles without overflowing.

hints.text: Rearrange the test so it uses only subtraction that cannot overflow.
For positive `b`, the sum overflows when `a` is above `INT_MAX - b`.
For `b` below zero, compare `a` with `INT_MIN - b`.

feedback.correct: Your check never overflows, so it stays defined on every input.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A test that calls `a + b` has already gone wrong.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check the return type and the `<climits>` names.

explain.text: Check before you do it: compare `a` with `INT_MAX - b` instead of adding. This app's compiler removes a check made after the addition. Another build might not, which is the point.

screens.title: What value is y?
screens.prose: The pricing course showed a check on `x + 1` change between `-O0` and `-O2`. Here is the plain case.
screens.question: What value does `y` hold?

options.text: No value is promised: the program is undefined

options.why: The hardware may wrap. C++ does not promise to pass that on.
There is no larger `int` to hold 2,147,483,648.
It compiles, and the compiler may warn if it can see the constants.

hints.text: Is signed overflow defined in C++?
Unsigned wraps. Signed does not.
With no defined result, the standard promises nothing about `y`, or about the rest of the run.

feedback.correct: No value is promised: signed overflow is undefined.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the standard defines signed overflow.

byKey.wrap: You assumed the hardware's wrap. C++ does not promise to pass that on.
byKey.big: There is no larger `int` to hold 2,147,483,648.
byKey.error: It compiles, and the compiler may warn if it can see the constants.

explain.text: Wrapping is what many CPUs do, but C++ promises nothing for a signed overflow. The optimiser may assume it never happens.

screens.title: The unsigned size
screens.prose: `v` is an empty `std::vector<int>`. Here `size_t` is 4 bytes. On a desktop it is 8.
screens.question: What does `v.size() - 1` equal here?

hints.text: What type does `size()` return?
An unsigned type cannot go below 0.
Zero minus one wraps to the largest 32-bit value.

feedback.correct: 4,294,967,295: defined, and the reason that loop never ends.

byKey.minus-one: You expected -1. `size()` is unsigned, so the subtraction wraps.

explain.text: Unsigned subtraction wraps, so 0 - 1 is 4,294,967,295 here and 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 on a desktop. It is defined, and `i >= 0` is always true, so the loop never ends.

screens.title: The defined check
screens.prose: For `add_overflows`, order the reasoning when `b` is positive. One line is the flawed habit.
screens.question: Put the lines in order, and leave the flawed one out.

lines.text: otherwise it overflows exactly when `a < INT_MIN - b`
compute `a + b` and compare it with `a`
lines.why: The addition has already overflowed, so there is nothing defined left to compare.

lines.text: the sum overflows exactly when `a > INT_MAX - b`

hints.text: Split on the sign of `b` first.
Each branch compares `a` with a limit shifted by `b`.
Positive `b` pushes up, so compare with `INT_MAX - b`.

feedback.correct: Split on the sign, then compare with a shifted limit. No sum is ever formed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide the branch before the test.

byKey.d1: You added first. The addition has already overflowed, so there is nothing defined left to compare.

explain.text: Each test uses a subtraction that stays in range. No line forms the sum, so the check is defined for every input.

screens.title: A comparator that breaks sort
screens.prose: `std::sort` assumes the comparator is a strict weak ordering. A comparator that breaks that makes the sort undefined.
screens.question: Which comparator makes `std::sort` undefined?

options.text: `[](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }`
`[](int a, int b) { return a < b; }`
options.why: Plain `<` is the model strict ordering.

options.text: `[](int a, int b) { return a > b; }`
options.why: A descending sort is fine: `>` is a strict ordering.

options.text: `[](int a, int b) { return std::abs(a) < std::abs(b); }`
options.why: Ties are allowed: equivalent elements compare false both ways.

hints.text: A comparator must return false for two equal elements.
Which option returns true for equal values?
`a <= b` says an element is less than itself.

feedback.correct: `<=` returns true for equal elements, so it is not a strict ordering.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what each comparator returns for two equal numbers.

byKey.lt: You picked plain `<`. It is the model strict ordering.
byKey.gt: You picked `>`. A descending sort is fine.
byKey.abs: You picked the absolute value. Ties compare false both ways, which is allowed.

explain.text: With `a <= b`, equal elements each count as less than the other. The algorithm's loops may then run off the end of the range, which is undefined.

screens.title: Check before, never after
screens.question: Your tests pass and the sanitiser is silent. Is the code free of undefined behaviour?

options.text: Only for the inputs run, on that build

options.why: Undefined behaviour belongs to the code for any input it can meet, and testing only samples inputs.
The sanitiser reports only what the run reaches.

feedback.correct: Tests and sanitisers sample inputs. They do not prove the absence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about inputs you did not run.

explain.text: A clean run says nothing about the inputs it never met. Write the check before the operation and keep the sanitiser in your tests as well.

screens.title: Summing fills in pence
screens.prose: A desk sums fill values in pence in an `int`. 5,000 fills of £5,000 are £25,000,000, that is 2,500,000,000 pence.
screens.question: What type should the total be?

options.why: It doubles the range to £42,949,672.95 and wraps silently.
It is exact for whole pence up to 2^53, but sums of money belong in integers.

options.text: Keep `int` and check after each addition
options.why: A check after the addition runs too late, as in the earlier overflow task.

hints.text: How many pence does an `int` hold?
It tops out at 2,147,483,647 pence, about £21 million.
Use a 64-bit integer: its range is far beyond any desk total.

feedback.correct: A 64-bit integer. An `int` holds only £21,474,836.47 of pence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. 2,500,000,000 pence is above the `int` limit.

byKey.unsigned: You chose `unsigned`. It doubles the range to £42,949,672.95 and wraps silently.
byKey.double: You chose `double`. Sums of money belong in integers.
byKey.check: You kept `int` and checked after. A check after the addition runs too late.

explain.text: An `int` holds up to 2,147,483,647 pence, which is £21,474,836.47. A signed overflow is undefined, so use `std::int64_t` and keep money in whole pence.

ideas: Undefined behaviour is not a bug that crashes: the standard puts no limit on the run, so the compiler assumes it never happens and may delete checks.
Signed overflow, an index past the end, an unset read and a shift by the width are undefined. Unsigned wrap-around and `-7 / 2` are defined.
Check before the operation, never after. Tests and sanitisers only sample inputs; use `-fsanitize=undefined` and wide types for money.

formula.name: Check before you do it
formula.note: Never form the sum you are testing.

summary.trap: Signed overflow does not wrap in C++. No value is promised, and the compiler may remove checks made afterwards.

quiz.question: Which statement about overflow is true?

options.text: Unsigned overflow wraps by definition; signed overflow is undefined
Both wrap, because the hardware does
options.why: C++ promises wrapping only for unsigned types.
It is the other way round.
Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One of the two is defined.

explain.text: The standard defines unsigned wrap-around. Signed overflow gets no promise.

quiz.question: Which flag finds undefined behaviour while the program runs?

options.why: It warns at compile time and cannot see values at run time.
It optimises. It reports nothing.
It picks a language version only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The check must run with the program.

explain.text: Use `-fsanitize=undefined` in tests, and `-fsanitize=address` for memory errors.

quiz.prose: `INT_MAX` is 2,147,483,647 and a price is held in pence.
quiz.question: What is `INT_MAX` pence in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A pound is 100 pence.

byKey.pence: You gave the pence figure. Divide by 100 to get pounds.

explain.text: 2,147,483,647 / 100 is 21,474,836.47 pounds. That is the most an `int` of pence can hold.

options.text: Undefined: index 4 is one past the end
Fine: the array has room for 4 numbers
options.why: An array of 4 has indices 0 to 3.
Indexing does not wrap.
It compiles. The standard just promises nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the valid indices.

explain.text: An array of 4 has indices 0 to 3, so `a[4]` is undefined even when it appears to work.
